questions: Does the 15 mm sensor spacing give a clean, monotonic signal across the full tape width, or are there dead zones or saturation?
Is a forward offset of 50 mm ahead of the axle enough lead for the bends, or does the signal arrive too late?
Is the 120 mm wheel track and 0.8 kg mass stable under the controller, or does yaw response cause oscillation?
Does the sensor row ever lose the line on the s-bend or slalom, and at what curvature?
feedback_request.requested_changes_if_any: None yet. Report which geometric parameter, if any, is the binding constraint.

intent: Establish a symmetric, evenly spaced 5-sensor baseline with a 12 mm footprint, placed 50 mm ahead of the axle. The Integrator can build a weighted-average controller on this row. Next iteration, I will adjust sensor spacing, forward offset and track width based on whether the robot loses the line on curves or oscillates on the slalom.
learning: Baseline only. No race data yet. The key open question is whether sensor spacing or forward lead is the limiting factor on curves, so the next revision should change one of these at a time.
rationale: Iteration 0 has no race telemetry and no Integration Feedback yet, so this proposal rests on the contract alone. A 5-sensor row spaced 15 mm apart covers the 25 mm tape at any lateral offset up to about 27 mm, so the line stays visible across the sensor array during moderate errors. Sensors sit 50 mm ahead of the axle so the signal leads the wheels, which helps on curves. The 12 mm footprint is small enough to resolve the edge of the tape without washing out the signal. The track is 120 mm, a middle value that gives a reasonable turn rate and yaw inertia without making the robot too twitchy. Mass is 0.8 kg, and the 30 mm wheel radius gives enough speed for the 1.5 m/s average the 3 s limit requires. Body width of 120 mm keeps the off-track limit at max(0.06, 0.0125+0.03)=0.0425 m, which is looser than the line itself. I expect a complete run on the development tracks, with the main risk being oscillation on the slalom because the sensor row is wide relative to the bends. This is a baseline for measurement, not a tuned design.
